metadata.title: The Average That Hides the Patient
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: how an aggregate calibration score can look perfectly acceptable while an AI model misses two out of three sepsis cases in a real hospital. Lands the carry-out that calibration metrics are weighted averages where the majority drowns out the vulnerable.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B08 / B09 (patient cloud collapsing into one aggregate ECE, then re-separating into off-diagonal subgroups)
metadata.one_flag: B10 — arithmetic washout (5% vulnerable subgroup diluted 20-to-1 by majority)

beats.narration_text: When an AI model's average calibration looks solid, does that mean every patient is protected? It doesn't. A calibration score is a weighted average, and an average can easily bury the patient who needs it most.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on 'safe for every patient?', corrects to 'hiding the patient who needs it?'

props.text:
If a clinical model's
average calibration looks fine,
is it safe for every patient?
props.replacementWords: hiding the patient who needs it?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Liam reads over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: In hundreds of hospitals, a proprietary AI model monitored patients around the clock for sepsis. On paper, across millions of aggregate records, its calibration and performance numbers looked perfectly acceptable.

shot.new_visual_element: Hospital bedside monitor card with aggregate sepsis detection metrics and internal validation seal

production_viz.label: The Hospital Sepsis Monitor
production_viz.mechanic: Bedside sepsis monitor card showing developer-reported AUC 0.76-0.83 and passed internal validation.

beats.narration_text: Then independent researchers externally validated it at Michigan Medicine. The model missed sixty-seven percent of sepsis cases. Two out of three patients who actually developed sepsis were completely overlooked.

shot.new_visual_element: External audit card: Wong et al. 2021 Michigan Medicine study, AUC 0.63, PPV 12%, 67% missed cases highlighted in terracotta

production_viz.label: The External Validation Audit
production_viz.mechanic: Audit scorecard displaying Wong et al. 2021 findings across 27,697 patients with 67% missed cases highlighted.

beats.narration_text: How does a model pass internal validation and fail so catastrophically on the floor? To see the arithmetic trap, look at how calibration is measured across a population.

shot.new_visual_element: Population cloud of patient dots under a global Expected Calibration Error gauge

production_viz.label: Anchor Planted: The Patient Cloud
production_viz.mechanic: Dense field of patient dots mapped beneath a global calibration error header.

beats.narration_text: The intuitive assumption is that an aggregate calibration score protects everyone equally. If the overall Expected Calibration Error is low, we assume predicted risks match real outcomes across the board.

shot.new_visual_element: Wrong guess card: Global Calibration = Universal Protection, struck through with terracotta slash

production_viz.label: Wrong Guess: Universal Safety
production_viz.mechanic: Assumption card claiming low global error guarantees universal protection, cancelled with terracotta strike.

beats.narration_text: That intuition fails because calibration error is a weighted sum. Every patient group contributes to the final number in proportion to its size. A majority subgroup dominates the arithmetic.

shot.new_visual_element: Weighted average balance: 85% majority cohort overwhelmingly tilting the aggregate scale against 5% high-risk cohort

production_viz.label: The Weighted Average Balance
production_viz.mechanic: Scale showing patient subgroup weight fractions: routine majority dwarfs high-risk minority.

beats.narration_text: In a standard reliability diagram, predictions are grouped into confidence bins. A well-calibrated model tracks the diagonal: patients given an eighty percent risk develop the condition eighty percent of the time.

shot.new_visual_element: Reliability diagram axes with 45-degree dashed diagonal line and calibrated risk bins

production_viz.label: The Reliability Diagram Diagonal
production_viz.mechanic: Predicted risk vs observed frequency diagram with perfect-calibration diagonal line.

beats.narration_text: On aggregate, the entire hospital population hugs that diagonal. The healthy majority and routine admissions smooth out the errors, creating the illusion of trustworthy probabilities.

shot.new_visual_element: Aggregate reliability curve tightly hugging the diagonal with Global ECE 0.018 tag

production_viz.label: Aggregate Smoothing
production_viz.mechanic: Hospital-wide curve hugging the diagonal line, producing low global ECE.

beats.narration_text: Watch what happens when the entire patient cloud collapses into a single aggregate metric. Thousands of individual patients pool into one neat, reassuring number. All subgroup distinction vanishes.

shot.new_visual_element: Patient dot cloud physically collapsing and pooling inward into a single compact Global ECE card

production_viz.label: The Collapse Move
production_viz.mechanic: Manim move collapse: patient dots pool inward into one single global ECE card.

beats.narration_text: Now, re-separate those same patients into clinical subgroups. The adult cohort stays on the diagonal. But look at the rare cases and high-risk patients: their predictions swing wildly off the line.

shot.new_visual_element: Decomposed subgroup curves: adult cohort on diagonal, rare-disease cohort swinging off-diagonal with severe miscalibration in terracotta

production_viz.label: Subgroup Decomposition Off Diagonal
production_viz.mechanic: Separate reliability curves for adult vs rare-disease cases showing off-diagonal departure.

beats.narration_text: A tiny subgroup can suffer catastrophic miscalibration with zero impact on the global score. In a cohort of ten thousand, a five percent group with broken probabilities moves the global error by a fraction of a percent.

shot.new_visual_element: Arithmetic washout card: 500 patients with 25% error diluted 20-to-1 by 9,500 routine patients

production_viz.label: The Arithmetic Washout
production_viz.mechanic: Card showing 20-to-1 arithmetic dilution of minority cohort miscalibration.

beats.narration_text: In one direction, relying on a global metric gives false assurance. Deploying a model without subgroup decomposition exposes vulnerable patient pools to blind spots hidden inside a clean summary.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction A card: Global Metric Only creates critical blind spots for vulnerable cohorts

production_viz.label: Direction A: The Global Blind Spot
production_viz.mechanic: Warning card on unexamined aggregate metrics masking clinical vulnerabilities.

beats.narration_text: In the other direction, requiring per-subgroup reliability curves reveals exactly where the model's probabilities hold and where human clinical oversight must step in.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction B card: Per-Subgroup Decomposition defines earned boundaries and necessary human oversight

production_viz.label: Direction B: Targeted Subgroup Audit
production_viz.mechanic: Protocol card showing verified reliability boundaries and human clinician handoff zones.

beats.narration_text: An aggregate calibration score doesn't tell you the model is safe for every patient — it tells you the majority is drowning out the vulnerable.

props.quote: An aggregate calibration score doesn't tell you the model is safe for every patient — it tells you the majority is drowning out the vulnerable.

beats.note: BCRY is the single carry-out sentence, serif, large.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take the predictive model your team uses in production. Look up its published calibration error or reliability curve. Now, break down the evaluation data by demographic, severity, or site cohorts. Check whether any subgroup's error is more than double the global average. Run that decomposition before your next deployment review. Liam, in for Bear.
